back: Examining, breaking down, synthesizing and clarifying information to understand, complete and improve it.

Determine analysis approach; create and analyze models; define and elaborate requirements; define acceptance criteria; verify; validate; prioritize; identify and analyze product risks; assess product design options.
A visual representation of information, as a diagram, table or structured text, that conveys a lot concisely.
Scope, process, rule, data, interface.
Context diagram, ecosystem map, event list, feature model, goal and business objectives model, organizational chart, use case diagram.
Process flow, use case, user story.
Business rules catalog, decision table, decision tree.
Data dictionary, data flow diagram, entity relationship diagram, state table and state diagram.
Prototype, wireframe, display-action-response model, report table, system interface table, user interface flow.
A scope model showing every system and person that interfaces directly with the solution, and the inputs and outputs between them.
A scope model showing all the relevant systems and the relationships between them. Wider than a context diagram.
A scope model showing all the features of a solution as a tree, with sub-features below each feature.
A picture of the steps people take in their work or with a solution. Also called a swim lane diagram or process map.
A text narrative of the interaction between a user and the system to reach a goal, with normal, alternative and exception flows.
As an (actor), I want to (function), so that I can (business reason).
User story: brief, a promise of a conversation, typical of adaptive work. Use case: detailed, every step and exception written out.
Not a process. It constrains or supports how the business behaves, and the solution must enforce it.
Tree: decisions as a branching flow, showing order. Table: every combination of conditions and its outcome.
A data model showing business data objects and the relationships between them, with cardinality.
A data model showing how data moves between external entities, data stores and processes.
A data model showing the valid states of an object and the allowed transitions between them.
Wireframe: a mock-up of one screen. User interface flow: how the user moves between screens.
Using several models together to find gaps, inconsistencies or redundancies.
All the product information together. Not necessarily a document: it can be a backlog or records in a tool.
Assumption: taken as true without proof. Constraint: a limiting factor on the development or implementation of the solution.
A well-refined backlog is detailed appropriately, estimated, emergent and prioritized.
Adding detail to a user story until it is ready for development. Also called backlog refinement. Done just in time.
Splitting an epic or story into smaller stories, each delivering value and small enough for one iteration.
Concrete and demonstrable conditions that must be met for the business stakeholders or customers to accept an item.
The behavior-driven development format for acceptance criteria: given the preconditions, when the user acts, then the product reacts.
Conditions the team agrees a user story must meet before work on it begins.
Conditions the team agrees an item must meet before it is considered complete and acceptable.
Checking that requirements are of sufficient quality: free of errors and conflicts, and meeting standards.
Checking that requirements meet the business goals and objectives.

front: Verify vs validate, in a phrase
back: Verify: are they written right? Validate: are they the right requirements?
Correct, complete, consistent.

front: Three peer reviews, least to most formal
back: Peer desk check, walkthrough, inspection.
A formal, rigorous review for completeness, consistency and conformance to standards, usually with a checklist.
Accountable stakeholders such as the product owner or sponsor decide. The business analyst facilitates and negotiates.
Business value from the business; effort and risk estimates from the team.
An uncertainty that can affect success in the definition, development or expected results of the product.

front: What does a product risk response often change?
back: The requirements: one is added or modified.
Identifying, analyzing and comparing design options against goals, cost, feasibility and risk, and recommending among them.
Requirements: what the product should do. Design: how it is built or looks.
Evaluating vendors and their products against a set of criteria, which can be weighted.
At least one before work begins. More than three: consider splitting the story.

front: Acceptance criteria versus definition of done
back: Acceptance criteria: one deliverable, story or feature. Definition of done: the whole product increment.
Roots and trunk: infrastructure. Branches: primary functions. Leaves: new features. Top priorities nearest the trunk; the rest may be pruned.
They state how the business operates whatever the technology. Requirements must support them.

front: How far does an analyst go toward design?
back: States what is required and refrains from specifying the technical design.
